title: Before the garden vote
paragraphs: Imagine a neighbourhood garden whose temporary agreement is about to expire. Each allotment has supplied some food, but the plots have also become places where neighbours exchange advice, rest after work and notice who has stopped coming. The committee now proposes a more competitive application process. Its stated aim is to widen access. That aim is reasonable; the question is whether the proposed method can recognise the different kinds of participation that the garden already supports, rather than rewarding only the easiest activity to count.

The proposed metric is the number of recorded visits. As a proxy for commitment, it has an obvious attraction: a list can be checked without asking anyone to judge another person’s motives. Yet a visit count also depends on how easily someone can reach the gate, sign the book or attend during opening hours. A person who coordinates watering by telephone may appear less active than someone who signs in frequently but contributes little. A transparent number does not automatically make the inference drawn from it transparent. Using several metrics would not remove that problem unless each one had a clear purpose.

The incumbent chair defends the plan by pointing to a mandate to improve access, not merely to preserve existing arrangements. That distinction matters. Continuity cannot mean that current users inherit permanent priority while newcomers wait indefinitely. Equally, the possibility of change does not remove the need to explain how its burdens will be distributed. A gardener with limited mobility may face a disproportionate loss from a rule that looks identical for everyone. Equal wording is not always the same as an equal practical opportunity.

Consultation is therefore more than collecting approval or disapproval after the essential choices have been fixed. It should expose which assumptions could still change and which constraints the committee believes it cannot change. Deliberation can then concern alternatives rather than the character of the people proposing them. An objection may defend a private advantage, identify an overlooked cost, or do both at once. Treating these possibilities as mutually exclusive would make discussion simpler at the price of making it less informative.

One participant offers a carefully framed preference: “I would rather the committee published its criteria before it voted.” The past form does not locate publication in an earlier year. It asks for a future sequence while avoiding the direct force of an instruction. That distance can help a difficult discussion, although it should not obscure who is expected to act. Nor does a tactful preference establish agreement. The chair may accept it, reject it or ask whether publication would actually leave enough time for meaningful responses.

Another speaker is less patient: “It is high time we stopped treating every objection as resistance to change.” This is a demand for a present change, not a report that the behaviour has already ended. Its urgency may be justified by the history of the discussion, but the wording also risks making listeners defensive. A more neutral invitation to examine particular objections could produce a better answer. The choice of grammar carries an attitude towards the audience as well as a description of the desired action.

Tenure adds another complication. If permission to use a plot is revocable at short notice, people may hesitate to improve its soil or organise long-term shared work. A promise of unlimited security, however, could prevent the access reform from achieving anything. The practical choice need not be between permanent possession and constant insecurity. A stated review period, clear reasons for withdrawal and a way to challenge an error might support planning while preserving the possibility of redistribution. The value lies in specifying the arrangement, not merely naming it fair.

A procedural improvement cannot guarantee a satisfying outcome for every gardener. It can make the grounds of a decision inspectable and show which evidence would justify reconsideration. The committee should therefore explain what its count can establish, what it leaves out and how exceptions will be considered. Such an account will be less tidy than a single ranking. It may also be more honest about a garden whose benefits include food, companionship and the shared work that makes both possible.
translation: 设想一个邻里菜园，临时使用协议即将到期。每块园地提供食物，也让邻居交流经验、下班休息，并留意谁已久未出现。委员会提议采用竞争更强的申请方式，目标是扩大准入。这个目标合理，但办法能否认识到菜园支持的不同参与方式，而不是只奖励最易计数的活动，仍需追问。
拟用的指标是登记到访次数。以它替代投入程度很方便：清单可核对，不必揣测动机。然而计数也受能否到门口、签到和在开放时段出席影响。通过电话协调浇水的人，可能看起来不如频繁签到却贡献不多的人活跃。数字透明，不等于由数字推得的结论也透明。除非每项指标都有清楚目的，使用多项指标本身也无法消除这个问题。
现任主席指出，授权是改善准入，而非只维护既有安排。这个区别重要：延续性不能意味着现有使用者永远优先、新人无限等待。但允许改变，也不能免除解释负担如何分配的责任。行动不便者可能因表面人人相同的规则承受过重损失。措辞相同不总意味着实际机会相同。
征询意见不只是基本选择定下后再收集赞成或反对，而应说明哪些假设还能改变、哪些限制被认为无法改变。审议才能讨论替代办法，而非评价提议者的人品。一项异议可能维护私利，也可能指出遗漏的成本，或兼具两者。把这些可能性说成互斥，会使讨论简单，却减少它提供的信息。
一位参与者谨慎表达偏好：“我更希望委员会在投票前公布标准。”过去式并非把公布放到往年，而是在要求未来的先后安排，同时减轻直接指令的力度。这种距离有时有助讨论，却不应模糊谁需要行动。委婉偏好也不证明已获同意，主席仍可接受、拒绝，或追问公布后是否留有足够回应时间。
另一人更急切：“我们早该停止把所有异议都当成抗拒改变了。”这要求现在改变，并非报告这种行为已经结束。讨论经历可能支持这种紧迫感，措辞也可能让听者戒备。更中性的邀请，逐项审视异议，也许能得到更好回应。语法选择既描述希望的行动，也表达对听众的态度。
使用期限与保障又添一层复杂性。若许可可在短时间内撤销，人们可能不愿改良土壤或组织长期合作。无限保障却可能使扩大准入毫无成效。实际选择未必只有永久占有或持续不安：写明复核周期、撤销理由和纠错途径，或能兼顾规划与重新分配。价值在于说清安排，而不只是称其公平。
程序改进无法保证每位种植者都满意，却能让决定根据可供审查，并说明什么证据值得重议。委员会应解释计数能说明什么、遗漏什么，以及如何考虑例外。这不如单一排名整齐，却可能更诚实地认识菜园的食物、陪伴和使二者成为可能的共同劳动。

grammar.surface: It is high time we stopped

questions.prompt: Which position best represents the essay’s argument?
options: Transparent criteria should examine what a metric measures and what a fair process must consider.
No change to current plot allocation can ever be justified.
A single visit count resolves every conflict about access.
questions.explanation: The essay supports examining access reform while questioning the inference from counts and specifying review, reasons and exceptions.

questions.prompt: Why does the telephone coordinator matter to the argument?
options: To prove that every frequent visitor contributes nothing.
To show that all recorded visits are invented.
To illustrate how meaningful participation may escape the chosen proxy.
questions.explanation: The example separates recorded presence from useful contribution; it neither rejects all records nor condemns all frequent visitors.

questions.prompt: What is the function of “I would rather the committee published its criteria before it voted”?
options: To document publication and voting that certainly happened last year.
To express a current preference about another actor’s future sequence.
To guarantee the chair’s agreement to the proposal.
questions.explanation: Paragraph five explicitly interprets the past form as a future preference with distance, not past evidence or established agreement.

questions.prompt: Why does the author contrast high time with a more neutral invitation?
options: To show that grammatical choices can convey urgency and affect listeners’ response.
To claim urgent wording is always dishonest.
To argue that the speakers can no longer discuss any objections.
questions.explanation: Paragraph six recognises potentially justified urgency while considering its interpersonal cost; it does not ban urgent language.

questions.prompt: In paragraph seven, what does revocable mean?
options: Able to be withdrawn under relevant conditions.
questions.explanation: The paragraph immediately links revocable permission to withdrawal at short notice and then considers review periods and stated reasons.

notes: 原创假设情境；文中提出的选择服务于语言和论证分析，不声称任何具体地区已经采用这些规则。
would rather带不同主语的过去式从句表达偏好；high time表达当下该做的行动并可能含批评，都不能仅凭过去式判定动作已完成。
预计阅读时间按160英语词/分钟向上取整，不是假设用户的个性化速度。
